questions.prompt: You add a stdio MCP server with `claude mcp add myserver -- <command>`. What is the most accurate description of what you did?
questions.explain: The server is a command the harness launches on your machine. Assume it can do what that command can do with the credentials you hand it, so it is a trust decision like installing any software.

options.text: Installed software that can use the credentials you give it
Added a text file of extra instructions that the model may ignore
options.misconception: That describes an instructions file or a Skill. A server runs code.

options.text: Switched on a feature that Anthropic checks before it can run
options.misconception: The docs tell you to verify that you trust each server before connecting it. The docs leave that check with you.

options.text: Opened a read-only view of the data, so nothing can change
options.misconception: Read-only belongs to a particular server or credential, and MCP itself makes no such promise.

questions.prompt: Where does each MCP server scope apply in Claude Code?
questions.explain: Local is the default and is not shared. Project lives in .mcp.json in version control. User follows you everywhere.

items.misconception: Local is the default and stays with you.
The file sits in the project root and is shared through version control.
User scope applies across every project you open.

items.text: A server stored in ~/.claude.json for this project alone
items.misconception: Local scope is kept in your own file and stays with you.

items.text: A server your teammates get when they clone the repository
items.misconception: Only the project scope travels with the repository.

items.text: A server added once with --scope user
items.misconception: User scope follows you into every project.

questions.prompt: You clone a repository and Claude Code asks whether to use a server from its .mcp.json. What is the sound reading?
questions.explain: The approval prompt is the gate for project-scoped servers. A committed .mcp.json asks to start software on your machine, so read it first.

options.text: Read it first: it asks to start code you did not write
It is harmless because anything in a repository has been reviewed
options.misconception: A repository can contain anything its authors committed. A repository carries no promise of review.

options.text: Approve it, because declining breaks the rest of the project
options.misconception: The prompt exists so you can say no. The risk lies in approving what you have not read.

options.text: The prompt only appears for servers that need credentials
options.misconception: The prompt covers project-scoped servers in general, whatever credentials they use.

questions.prompt: A teammate lists habits for adding a server. Which line is the unsafe one?
questions.explain: Servers that fetch external content can expose you to prompt injection, so verify trust before connecting. Handing it write credentials and letting it act unattended removes the checks.

lines.text: Check who publishes the server and what tools it lists
lines.why: Reading before adding is the first check.

lines.text: Choose a read-only server where one exists
lines.why: A server that cannot write limits what injected text can do.

lines.text: Give it a write token and let it run unattended on fetched pages
Remove servers you no longer need, since tools use context
lines.why: MCP tools consume model context, so add only what you need.

questions.prompt: Match each risk to the habit that shrinks it.
questions.explain: Each habit puts a limit between the server and the damage it could do.

pairs.left: Fetched text tells the agent to write somewhere
pairs.misconception: Injection is answered by limiting what the agent can do with that text.

pairs.left: The token you gave the server has broad scope
pairs.right: Limit the token to what the job needs
pairs.misconception: A broad token widens the damage of any mistake or injected instruction.

pairs.left: A cloned repo ships a project server
pairs.misconception: The approval prompt only helps if you have read what it asks to start.

pairs.left: A dangerous tool on a server you need
pairs.right: Deny that tool by its mcp__ name
pairs.misconception: Rules match tool names, so one tool can be refused while the rest stay usable.

questions.prompt: A public registry lists an MCP server that many people have installed. What does the listing tell you about its safety?
questions.explain: A listing tells you it is easy to find. A registry can list self-reported data and run no security review, so check the maintainer, the review date and what the server may do.

options.text: Only that it is listed, which says nothing about review
That registry staff have reviewed its code for security
options.misconception: A registry can list self-reported data without any security review.

options.text: That so many installs mean others have already vetted it
options.misconception: Popularity is not vetting, and a popular server can carry hidden instructions in its tool descriptions.

options.text: That it is safe if it only reads, since reading cannot be abused
options.misconception: Read-only helps, but text it returns can still carry injected instructions.
